title: Task-Aware Early Termination for HNSW via Label-Histogram Stabilization

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reduce HNSW search latency when downstream tasks only need label correctness, not exact neighbor identities. Paper [2] discusses improving ANN search efficiency through adaptive early termination, which aligns with the same objective of reducing latency in approximate nearest neighbor search. While [2] does not specifically focus on HNSW or label correctness, the broader purpose of latency reduction in ANN search is substantively equivalent.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces a training-free early exit criterion based on the L1 distance between consecutive top-K label histograms, terminating when the difference falls below a K-scaled threshold. Paper [12] proposes a learned early exit mechanism for speeding up inference, but it relies on learned exits rather than a training-free heuristic. Paper [22] introduces Confidence-Guided Early Stopping (CGES), which adaptively halts sampling based on posterior mass accumulation, but this mechanism is Bayesian and does not involve histogram-based thresholds. Paper [10] discusses a reliability-based stopping criterion for iterative decoding, but it operates on Log-Likelihood Ratios (LLRs) rather than label histograms. None of these papers use the same primitive mechanism of computing L1 distance between label histograms for early exit, making the mechanism novel.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates latency reduction and label recall on the Iceberg ImageNet-EVA02 benchmark. Paper [9] describes ANN-Benchmarks, a tool for evaluating ANN algorithms on standard datasets, which includes latency and recall metrics. While the specific benchmark (Iceberg ImageNet-EVA02) is new, the evaluation design — measuring latency reduction and recall on a benchmark dataset — is substantively equivalent to the benchmarking approach in [9]. Paper [2] also evaluates latency reduction and recall in ANN search, further confirming that the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of approximate nearest neighbor search. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], and [7] all address approximate nearest neighbor search, covering this domain comprehensively.

**PURPOSE: Reduce HNSW search latency when downstream tasks only need label correctness, not exact neighbor identities.**

Paper [2] is the closest: it addresses "Improving Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search through Learned Adaptive Early Termination" — the objective is reducing ANN search latency via early termination. However, its purpose is general ANN latency reduction, not specifically exploiting the weaker requirement of label correctness (task-sufficiency) rather than exact neighbor identity. Paper [6] analyzes HNSW efficiency but doesn't target label-only correctness. No prior paper specifically frames the purpose as "the downstream task only needs label correctness, so we can exit earlier than exact-neighbor convergence." This is a distinct objective — exploiting task-level sufficiency to reduce search effort — not merely "speed up ANN search." Paper [2]'s purpose is general latency reduction without the label-sufficiency framing. The gap being closed here is specifically that fixed efSearch wastes computation when label convergence precedes neighbor-identity convergence — no prior paper targets this specific gap.

**PURPOSE verdict: NONE** — no prior paper pursues the same objective of exploiting label-correctness sufficiency (as opposed to neighbor-identity convergence) to terminate HNSW early.

---

**MECHANISM: Training-free early exit criterion computing L1 distance between consecutive top-K label histograms at checkpoints, terminating when below a K-scaled threshold.**

Paper [2] uses a *learned* adaptive early termination for ANN search — it trains a model to predict when to stop. The contribution's mechanism is explicitly *training-free* and uses label histogram stability (L1 distance between consecutive histograms). Paper [10] uses a reliability-based stopping criterion for iterative decoding based on LLR thresholds — different domain, but the primitive is "monitor a stability signal across iterations and stop when it crosses a threshold." Paper [22] (CGES) monitors posterior mass accumulation over LLM samples and stops when confidence is sufficient — similar "monitor convergence of a distribution and stop" primitive. Paper [25] (Anytime Heuristic Search) uses anytime algorithms that stop based on solution quality signals. None of these use the specific primitive of computing L1 distance between consecutive top-K label histograms. The closest structural analog is [2], but its mechanism is learned (not training-free) and doesn't use histogram comparison. The histogram-stability-as-stopping-criterion primitive applied to ANN graph traversal is not present in any prior paper.

**MECHANISM verdict: NONE** — no prior paper uses L1 distance between consecutive top-K label histograms as a training-free stopping criterion for graph-based ANN search.

---

**EVALUATION: Iceberg ImageNet-EVA02 benchmark, p50/p99 latency reduction vs fixed-efSearch baselines, Label Recall@100 within 0.01 pp.**

Paper [9] (ANN-Benchmarks) establishes the standard evaluation design for ANN algorithms: measure recall vs. latency tradeoffs on standard datasets. Paper [1] surveys ANN benchmarking approaches. The evaluation design here — measuring recall (Label Recall@100) and latency (p50/p99) against a fixed-parameter baseline on a standard ANN benchmark — follows the same design as [9]: recall-latency tradeoff on a named benchmark. The specific benchmark (Iceberg ImageNet-EVA02) is a different instance, but the evaluation design (recall metric + latency metric + comparison to baseline on a named benchmark) is the same family as [9]. Per the special rule, swapping the benchmark instance doesn't make the evaluation novel.

**EVALUATION verdict: 9** — ANN-Benchmarks establishes the recall-vs-latency evaluation design on named benchmarks.

**DOMAIN: Approximate nearest neighbor search.**

Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [9] all operate in the approximate nearest neighbor search domain explicitly.

**DOMAIN verdict: 1** (and 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 — citing [1] as representative).
